findings.passage: Ellison has explained more than once why, in 1977, he co-founded the company that became Oracle, and the reason does not change.
findings.problem: The body never orients a reader who does not already know him. This is the first body mention of Oracle and the article never says what Oracle sells, how large it became, or why Bill Gates and Microsoft were the rival. His scale arrives only in asides ("by then one of the richest people alive", "for a man of his wealth"). The opening list of yachts, fighter jet, island and the Gates war assumes the reader knows all of it, so the stakes of the admired-versus-respected question are borrowed from prior knowledge.
findings.acceptance_test: Before the type H2 or at this first Oracle mention, a reader with no prior knowledge can say in one sentence what Oracle makes, that it made Ellison one of the richest people in the world, and why Gates/Microsoft was his rival. Use only facts in the opened record (for example S01's 1995 company size, S07's 2000 wealth race with Gates); do not add an unsourced net-worth figure. The sister-story opening stays first.

findings.passage: In June 2000 it emerged that a detective firm hired by Oracle had tried to buy the office trash of a Microsoft-funded trade group. Ellison could have blamed the contractor.
findings.problem: The centerpiece episode has no stated purpose. The reader is not told why Oracle wanted a trade group's trash or what was going on between Microsoft and the government at the time, so "information that was hidden", "a public service" and the critic's "front groups of its own" cannot be weighed. Without the motive the reader cannot judge the section's key claim that he "could look better or concede nothing", because it is unclear what conceding would have meant.
findings.acceptance_test: One or two sourced sentences state what Oracle said it was trying to find and why it mattered in 2000 (the trade group's ties to Microsoft and the dispute it was part of), drawn from an opened source. If the opened sources do not support the backdrop, say plainly what they do establish and open one that does. After the fix a new reader can explain what Ellison was accused of and what he claimed in defense.

findings.passage: His politics drew a protest inside his own company. He called himself "a lifelong Democrat" in 2002.
findings.problem: From here to the Oracle co-CEO paragraph the profile turns into a dated list: Trump fundraiser, November 2020 call, Lanai, Twitter, the guarantee, the lawsuit, the title change. Several items carry no sentence on what they show about him, and the move from "lifelong Democrat" to hosting a Trump fundraiser is stated and dropped. The section heading promises the surveillance contradiction but half the section is unrelated to it. References assume knowledge: True the Vote is unexplained, the reader is never told Warner Bros. Discovery owned CNN (so the spokesperson's CNN denial comes from nowhere), and the company is called Paramount Skydance, Paramount and Skydance within three paragraphs. Momentum built by the storm and the type argument is lost in the last third.
findings.acceptance_test: Every controversy stays on the page, but each paragraph either ties the episode to the control-versus-approval question in one clearly labeled interpretive sentence or says plainly that the record shows nothing about motive. The party shift is either addressed with sourced evidence or flagged as unexplained. Section headings match their contents. Each unfamiliar name gets a one-clause identification, the CNN link is explained as the complaint frames it (S23), and the company rename is stated once. A new reader can say why each paragraph is in the profile.

findings.passage: HP disputed his account of the board's vote. Oracle hired Hurd the next month.
findings.problem: The reader is not told who Mark Hurd was (HP's chief executive), why HP forced him out, or what account of a board vote Ellison gave; the quoted email says nothing about a vote, so the dispute sentence dangles. Without the reason for Hurd's exit the reader cannot see why defending him cost approval, which is the point of the bullet, or why hiring him was "a coup against a competitor".
findings.acceptance_test: The bullet names Hurd's role, gives HP's stated reason for his exit as S14 reports it (including that the harassment claim was not substantiated by HP's board), and either states the specific claim HP disputed or drops that sentence.

findings.passage: Prosecutors then charged Lee over an email offered as evidence.
findings.problem: The paragraph turns on an email the reader never sees described. It does not say what the email purported to show, who was supposed to have sent it, or why a jury found it false, so the defense theory that it was "planted" and the later line that "the conviction concerned the forged email" are hard to follow. On a sensitive allegation the reader should be able to state both sides' positions from the page.
findings.acceptance_test: A reader can say what the email claimed, who it was attributed to and on what basis the jury rejected it, attributed to S11 with its stated limit (it leans on Softwar and gives Ellison's side more fully). No new characterisation of Lee or Ellison is added beyond the source.

findings.passage: Asked in 1997 whether he had ever been deeply afraid, he said only once, at about six, when his mother came home late from work
findings.problem: Family references are ambiguous for a new reader. The article says his birth mother gave him up at nine months to her aunt and uncle, then refers to "his mother" and, from the first line, "his sister" without saying who they are. A reader cannot tell whether the feared loss is the adoptive mother or the birth mother, at the exact point the article says the memory "sit[s] close to what his sister was asking".
findings.acceptance_test: At first mention the text identifies the mother in this memory and the sister in the opening story by their relation to him (adoptive family or otherwise) if an opened source supports it; if the sources do not specify, the text says so in a clause. No names or dates are added without a source.

findings.passage: His yacht Sayonara entered the Sydney to Hobart race and sailed into a storm that killed six sailors on other boats.
findings.problem: The section never says Ellison was aboard. A new reader learns he was in danger only two sections later ("nearly dying at sea"). The heading says the storm "found his limit" and the close says he "met a real limit", but the section gives no account of what he went through, only the result and his later reflections.
findings.acceptance_test: The section states he was sailing on the boat and gives one sourced first-person detail of the danger (S10 has "We were at our absolute limits in this storm."), so the heading and the closing line are earned by what the reader has been shown. The closing two sentences of the section stay.

findings.passage: In the USC speech he described his first wife divorcing him after he wanted to buy a sailboat, which she took as proof he lacked ambition.
findings.problem: This is the only example under the bolded discriminator, and a new reader cannot see how it shows "the reverse" of adjusting to protect how he is seen. She left him; he is not shown choosing control at a cost. The stronger examples (the trash press conference, Milken, Hurd) sit in the previous section and are not recalled here, so the argument's deciding step reads as a non sequitur.
findings.acceptance_test: The paragraph either explains in one sentence what he refused to change and what it cost him, or leads with the already-established public examples and uses the sailboat story as a supporting private case. A reader can restate the discriminator and name the evidence for it after reading this paragraph alone.

findings.passage: Jobs did not explain the joke. Ellison's own version is the story about his sister. In both tellings the boy says he would rather have standing than love, she tells him he is wrong, and the man telling the story agrees with her.
findings.problem: Two gaps in the ending. First, the article does not explain the joke either: a reader who does not know that "Rosebud" is the dying word in Citizen Kane gets nothing from the closing image. Second, the reader has not seen Ellison agree with his sister in the CBS telling. The CBS quotation in the opening stops at "walks out"; the agreement ("It took me a little while to realize that all of us want to be loved.") is in S04 but not in the draft, so "in both tellings" is unsupported by what is on the page.
findings.acceptance_test: One clause says what Rosebud is in the film, without claiming to know what Jobs meant by it. The CBS telling in the opening includes or accurately reports his follow-on sentence from S04, so the final paragraph's "in both tellings" matches text the reader has read.

protected_passages.passage: Admired in one telling, respected in the other. It could be a slip of memory forty years on. It is also the open question about him.
protected_passages.reason: The hook works with no prior knowledge. A one-word difference between two sourced tellings becomes the question the whole profile answers, and the article admits the dull explanation first.

protected_passages.passage: His conclusion: "I can run a company out of business all by myself. So I thought, next time, if the company was going to go down, I was going to be out front."
protected_passages.reason: The most memorable piece of evidence in the profile. It is funny, in his own words, and shows the control motive without the author having to assert it.

protected_passages.passage: His answer to fear is to get his hands on the controls. He says nothing there about how failure would look.
protected_passages.reason: States the discriminator in plain language right after the quotation that supports it. A reader new to the Enneagram understands the Eight-versus-Three difference from these two sentences.

protected_passages.passage: It is a joke. It also reads as an accurate self-portrait: a man who met a real limit, respected it, and still left himself an opening.
protected_passages.reason: Draws a specific insight out of a sourced joke and hedges it properly ("reads as"). The best section ending in the draft.

protected_passages.passage: An Eight at ease can be gentle, so some of this fits. A six-year-old afraid his mother will not come home fits every type equally. It is better left unexplained.
protected_passages.reason: The article declines to force a childhood memory into the type. That restraint makes the rest of the argument more believable to a skeptical new reader.

assessment: Read cold, the profile has a strong spine for its first two thirds. The sister story gives a new reader a real question, the founding quotation and the fear-of-failure answer give a clear and well-hedged argument, the Type 3 case is argued from his own words instead of being waved off, and the storm section is the best scene. A reader finishes knowing something specific: what he reaches for when afraid, and that he keeps choosing the unpopular position. Three things weaken it for someone who does not already know him. The body never says what Oracle is or how big he is, so the stakes are assumed. The trash episode, which carries the most weight, is told without its purpose. And the last third becomes a dated list of controversies with thin connection to the portrait, where unexplained names (Hurd, True the Vote, CNN, three versions of the company name) pile up. The remaining findings are cheap clarity repairs: the forged email, which mother and which sister, whether he was on the boat, the sailboat example under the discriminator, and an ending that leans on an unexplained film reference and on a CBS sentence the reader was never shown. Similarity advisory: available and not tripped (max 0.024 against a 0.04 threshold, no shared phrases). The top pairs are coincidental word overlap; I compared the arguments and found no reuse. The admired-versus-respected frame, the control-of-environment founding motive and the storm material are specific to this subject. Risk flags: sensitive allegations are present (the Adelyn Lee case, the insider-trading suit, the November 2020 call, the unresolved 2026 shareholder complaint) and the typing is contested by the article's own account (medium confidence, a strong Type 3 case, two unread biographies). I did not reopen sources; quotation checks here are limited to comparing the draft against the excerpts in the evidence record.
